title: Observations on Allegory in the Existentialist "Nightmare Realm" of I Saw The TV Glow (2024)

commenti.body:
I liked the movie too. I thought it was fairly pessimistic though. To me, it offers this tantalizing feeling that Owen is not who he is supposed to be, that he can be happy by becoming his "true self," but it never confirms the existence of that true self. It always remains possible that there is no true self to be had, that he is simply fixated on media he watched as a child, that there will be no moment of euphoria when Owen finally becomes himself.

I think the movie succeeds because of how well it shows that tantalizing feeling, and how it refuses to accept a simple, positive solution for Owen. There is no unearned catharsis.

The biggest flaw with the movie is that Owen is described as having a family in the voice-over, but the movie never attempts to show you his family, and it's impossible for me to imagine him as a father/husband.

I saw the voice over representing a tv-style "where are they now" flash forward. I thought all of it was fake, especially the rewriting of the pink opaque as a children's TV show. I interpreted that as the villain forcing Owen into the new role we see them in at the end - dead end job, miserable, dying. That feeling was exacerbated for me by the lack of aging during that time skip, and how empty the world felt during it. The only parts of the movie that felt "real" to me were the ones where other people existed with agency - the school scene at the beginning, the bar where Owen and Maddie meet with a punk band... The rest felt like a constructed fake world to keep Owen in line (grocery store, arcade, movie theater). 


I really wonder what it would have felt like to see Owen with a family that was as dysfunctional as their job.

A lot of these critiques are of things that are working as intended... 

Becoming trans or really accepting any queer identity can often feel apocalyptic. There is a real sense you might be destroying your life that you have in the name of what feels like a hypothetical. 

Similarly, Owen's invisible family is really meant to make his whole line of them being the most important thing to him clearly shallow and at minimum lacking in nuance.

>Similarly, Owen's invisible family is really meant to make his whole line of them being the most important thing to him clearly shallow and at minimum lacking in nuance

What does this mean? You think he's mistaken that he cares about his family?

The point is that it's a lie and a justification for why he doesn't try to go back to the the PO/transition. Obviously in real world terms he would have some love and care for his family, but not showing them and allowing us to see that allows the audience to see the claim as a facade.

Are you claiming that he doesn't really have a family? Or that they aren't really the most important thing to him?

If he has a family, I think the movie should show them to us. But I don't see the Owen as capable of handling the role of husband/father so it's peculiar.

This is my main quibble with the movie. I liked it otherwise.

Okay let me explain it this way. 

There is a gay guy married to a woman with three kids 

Deep down, he really wants to be his true self 

He knows that will likely lead to divorce and hurt his wife and radically change his life 

He loves his family 

He uses “my family is the most important thing to me” as a justification for not coming out. But of course he could have come out earlier. The story that he can’t come out because of his family is kinda bs because he’s spent his whole life coming up with other justifications for not coming out 

But that is a very complex thing to get across in a film. So, the movie chooses to not show you his family so the statement feels stilted, unearned, and not entirely true. It in short gets the vibes across

It's a completely understandable scenario but I think if you are putting that scenario in a movie you need to say more about the family apart from a throwaway line. It feels like a cheat otherwise. You're saying "it's supposed to feel like a cheat," but I'm thinking it's too much of a cheat.

I also think you're ignoring that this movie is about a specific person who does not display the emotional range required to be a father/husband. So when he says that line, you're like "wait, what?" A family indicates emotional reserves that the movie has not shown Owen to have.

If the movie isn't willing to show us his family or at least say more about his family, the line should have been cut. It would be better without it.

> The biggest flaw with the movie is that Owen is described as having a family in the voice-over, but the movie never attempts to show you his family, and it's impossible for me to imagine him as a father/husband.


He says it *as he brings the new TV in*
Are you saying his family is stuff he watches on TV? That would make sense
I am almost certain of it
